clue.text: An incomparable personal impression

parts.note: an impression made by one person alone, matching nobody else's, as left by a fingertip on glass

explanation.surface: Someone leaves a unique, unforgettable impression on others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impression' suggests the effect a person has on others; here it is a literal mark pressed onto a surface, unique to each person.
explanation.definitionFit: Each person's fingertip ridges leave a mark that no other person's matches, a literal impression unique to its owner.

clue.text: Good for nothing!

parts.note: read as a description of a lazy person who is of no use, rather than an exclamation of scorn

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry at something useless.
explanation.definitionFit: A layabout who does no work is called a good-for-nothing, a lazy loafer.

clue.text: Handled explosive

parts.note: an explosive thrown by hand, the 'hand' kind of bomb, rather than an explosive that has been dealt with

explanation.surface: A bomb disposal team has dealt with a dangerous device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handled' looks like 'dealt with', but points to the hand variety of this thrown bomb.
explanation.definitionFit: The small bomb thrown by a soldier is commonly called a hand grenade, an explosive meant to be handled.

clue.text: Word of compliance within Brighton's borders

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to something inside the limits of the seaside town Brighton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'within' signals the answer hidden in bRIGHTOn: Brighton less its first and last letters. BRIGHTON is an English seaside town.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'right-oh' is a casual British way of agreeing, an expression of assent.

clue.text: Encouraged by getting a break

definitions.meaning: heartened, freed from worry, cheered up
taken off duty when someone else takes over a watch or shift

explanation.surface: Someone feels heartened by being given time off.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone eased of anxiety feels heartened, and a sentry replaced at the end of a watch has been given respite.

clue.text: Opening under the bridge

parts.note: the bridge is that of the nose, and below it lie the two air passages

explanation.surface: A gap or passage beneath a river crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' suggests a river crossing; it is the bony bridge of the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the two air passages at the base of the nose is an opening lying beneath the nasal bridge.

clue.text: Rugby players-not half!

definitions.meaning: the four backs who line up between the half-backs and the full-back in rugby
read literally: a fraction that is more than a half, such as 75 per cent

explanation.surface: An emphatic exclamation about rugby players, using the slang 'not half!' for 'very much so'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'absolutely!', but here it is read literally: a fraction that is not a half.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby the backs between half-backs and full-back carry this name, and 75 per cent is a fraction other than a half.

clue.text: Hyperion's big sister?

parts.note: Hyperion was one of the giant Titans of Greek myth, so his sisters were female giants of that race

explanation.surface: A question about the older sister of someone named Hyperion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big' looks like 'older' but means giant: Hyperion's sisters, such as Theia and Rhea, were female Titans.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyperion was a Titan of Greek myth, so each of his sisters was a female member of that giant race.

clue.text: Naive enquiry from a new student at dental school

definitions.text: Naive enquiry from a new student at dental school

parts.words: Naive enquiry from a new student at dental school
parts.note: a newcomer asking for the routine, with a pun on the dentist's tool

explanation.surface: A fresher at dental school innocently asks a question.
explanation.walkthrough: The everyday phrase asks what the usual procedure is; at a dental school the newcomer could be asking about the tool used on teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is how a newcomer asks for the routine procedure, and dentistry is the trade of the tooth-boring tool.

clue.text: One who orchestrated everything he covered

indicators.note: the word he is placed around the synonym, covering it

parts.note: taken as written
everything means all

explanation.surface: A conductor arranged all the music he took on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covered' puts ALL inside HE. Sir Charles Halle founded Manchester's Halle Orchestra in 1858.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Halle, a pianist and conductor, founded and led a famous Manchester orchestra.

clue.text: Writer of work carrying a hall-mark

definitions.meaning: Oliver ..., the Irish author of The Vicar of Wakefield
a craftsman whose precious-metal pieces are stamped with an assay office mark

explanation.surface: An author whose writing bears a distinctive stamp.
explanation.walkthrough: A hallmark is the stamp an assay office puts on gold and silver; the writer is Oliver Goldsmith, the 18th-century Irish author.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Goldsmith wrote She Stoops to Conquer, and a craftsman in gold produces pieces that are stamped by the assay office.

clue.text: Three yuan traded for a Weber overture

indicators.note: traded means swapped about, so the letters change places

explanation.surface: Three Chinese coins are exchanged for a piece of music by Weber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'traded' rearranges THREE YUAN. Carl Maria von Weber wrote the opera Euryanthe, whose overture is often played alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Weber's 1823 opera of that name has an overture that is a concert favourite.

clue.text: By no means unhappy changing train

indicators.note: changing means altering, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller is perfectly content to switch trains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' rearranges TRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a literary term for laughing or cheerful, which is the opposite of sad.

clue.text: One in line for a remedy, say

definitions.text: One in line for a remedy, say

parts.words: One in line for a remedy, say
parts.note: someone standing in a waiting line, at the chemist's for medicine for example

explanation.surface: A patient waits their turn for medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks an example: waiting for a remedy is just one reason to stand in line.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who waits in a line for a turn is described by the noun formed from the verb for lining up.

clue.text: European from whom a schoolboy takes in a point

indicators.note: the schoolboy absorbs the point, so it goes inside him

parts.note: an Etonian is a pupil of Eton College, the English public school
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A European in whose company a schoolboy grasps an idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes in' puts S inside ETONIAN. ETON is a famous English boarding school, and 'point' is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Estonia, a Baltic state, is a European.

clue.text: An alarming temporary shelter?

parts.note: alarming read as 'like an alarm', which is a bell, describing a camping shelter of that shape

explanation.surface: A frightening place to sleep for the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alarming' looks like 'frightening', but means bell-like, since a bell is an alarm; the tent is bell-shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: A conical tent with a single central pole is named for its bell shape, and is a portable camping shelter.

clue.text: Certain to be quite breathless

definitions.meaning: read literally: surely without breath, having died

explanation.surface: Someone who is sure to be out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breathless' suggests panting; read literally it is someone no longer breathing, who is dead, and certainly so.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means utterly convinced, and someone who has stopped breathing is certainly deceased.

clue.text: Having given evidence.

parts.note: a plain description of someone or something that has borne witness or confirmed a fact

explanation.definitionFit: To bear witness or certify a fact formally is to provide proof of it, so a confirmed fact has been vouched for.

clue.text: One riding on the crest of a wave

definitions.text: One riding on the crest of a wave

parts.words: One riding on the crest of a wave
parts.note: the idiom for a successful person read literally, as someone who works or plays in breaking waves

explanation.surface: A person enjoying a run of great success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the crest of a wave' is an idiom for success; read literally it is someone in the breaking sea, a lifeboatman or surf-rider.
explanation.definitionFit: A man skilled in handling boats through breaking sea waves rides the crests of those waves.

clue.text: swears it could be the fish

indicators.note: the letters of swears could be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Someone swears that a creature is the fish in question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it could be' rearranges SWEARS.
explanation.definitionFit: The wrasse is a brightly coloured sea fish of rocky coasts.

clue.text: Head of the house?

parts.note: head read as the topmost part of a building rather than the person in charge of a household

explanation.surface: A question about who rules the household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of the house' suggests the householder; here it is the highest point of the building.
explanation.definitionFit: The topmost outer surface of a building is its summit, the house's highest part.

clue.text: Early ascetic emerging from German town, note

parts.note: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr, Germany
E is a note of the musical scale

explanation.surface: A hermit of ancient times comes out of a German town, so a note says.
explanation.walkthrough: The Essenes were a Jewish ascetic sect of the time of Christ, linked with the Dead Sea Scrolls.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of an ancient Jewish sect living a strict, self-denying communal life was an early ascetic.

clue.text: Key man of note

parts.note: a man who works on the keys and notes of a piano, setting its pitch, rather than an important celebrity

explanation.surface: An important, famous person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key man of note' reads as a prominent figure; it is the person who adjusts piano keys so each note sounds true.
explanation.definitionFit: A piano technician adjusts strings so that each key gives a true note.

clue.text: Ignominy of a tribute from Pluto

indicators.note: the tribute comes from Pluto, so his name is placed before it

parts.note: Dis is the Roman name for Pluto, god of the underworld
an honour is a tribute paid to someone

explanation.surface: The shame of being paid a compliment by the god of the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' puts DIS (Pluto) ahead of HONOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Public shame and loss of respect is disgrace, the same as ignominy.

clue.text: They are instrumental for hungry men of honour

definitions.text: They are instrumental for hungry men of honour

parts.words: They are instrumental for hungry men of honour
parts.note: men of honour are OBEs, holders of the British order; hungry ones have nothing, an O, inside them

explanation.surface: Some people help the starving recipients of national honours.
explanation.walkthrough: An OBE is an Officer of the Order of the British Empire, a British honour. Put O (nothing, so hungry) inside OBES and you get the woodwind instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Double-reed woodwind instruments of the orchestra are instrumental in the literal sense.

clue.text: Bat after the last one of the farmhouse pests

parts.note: the rear is the last part, the very back
a mouse is a common farm pest

explanation.surface: A bat goes after the final mouse plaguing a farmhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bat' looks like a verb, as if hitting a pest; it is the flying mammal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearmouse, or reremouse, is an old English dialect name for the flying mammal.

clue.text: Mythical creature with time to be revolutionary

parts.note: to roll is to revolve, turning over and over

explanation.surface: A creature of legend, given time, joins a revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' suggests politics; here it means turning in revolutions, rolling.
explanation.definitionFit: A troll is an ugly giant or dwarf of Scandinavian folklore.

clue.text: To do so may produce a very faint likeness

definitions.text: To do so may produce a very faint likeness

parts.words: To do so may produce a very faint likeness
parts.note: a photographer giving film too little light ends up with a pale, barely visible picture

explanation.surface: Some action that results in a portrait which hardly resembles its subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faint likeness' suggests a poor resemblance; it is a photograph too pale from too little light.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving photographic film too little light makes a pale, weak picture of the subject.
